articles.title: Leaked Keys: SaaS API Cost Attribution Explained Through Refusal Drills
articles.excerpt: A B2B SaaS leaked-key drill should end with an owner, an attributed usage record, and a decision about which traffic to refuse. Start with one key per cost centre and the platform's per-key usage figu…
articles.body: A B2B SaaS leaked-key drill should end with an owner, an attributed usage record, and a decision about which traffic to refuse. Start with one key per cost centre and the platform's per-key usage figures. The bill contains accepted API work and retained accounting evidence; asking teams to reconstruct consumption afterward adds a dispute to the response process. TL;DR: Attribute API costs across teams using keys as cost centres, rather than self-reported usage. Keep the spend-ceiling decision separate: attribution explains accepted work, while admission policy determines refused traffic. A shared service still needs an allocation rule. Quantify the exposure before choosing a control.
articles.author: AldenCross6847

articles.body: TL;DR: Personal, project, plugin, and managed Skills are not four tiers of one inheritance stack. They are different distribution contracts. Personal Skills favor local iteration; project Skills travel with reviewed repository changes; plugins add a namespace, versioned packaging, and other components; managed Skills support organization-wide deployment. The Agent Skills format is portable, but each runtime still has its own dependencies and sharing rules. Update for current Claude Code: Skills enabled in a claude.ai account can now sync down into signed-in terminal and cloud sessions; locally authored Skills are not automatically uploaded back to claude.ai. Part 8: From Loading to Compaction followed a Skill through a session.

articles.title: Building a Safe-by-Design HTTP Telemetry Crate in Rust
articles.excerpt: Incidents are easier to investigate when you can see what happened inside your HTTP service: which route failed, how long it took, and what the request looked like. But logging request data can create…
articles.body: Incidents are easier to investigate when you can see what happened inside your HTTP service: which route failed, how long it took, and what the request looked like. But logging request data can create new problems. Passwords and tokens may end up in logs. Large payloads can consume memory. And if telemetry export waits on a slow or unavailable backend, it can affect the request path. To address these tradeoffs, I built safe-http-telemetry, an open-source Rust crate for Axum and Tower applications. Its design goal is to make HTTP telemetry useful while keeping capture, resource use, and export behavior under the application’s control.

articles.title: How selfie search for event photos works, and what happens to the face data
articles.excerpt: After any big event (a wedding, a conference, a 10K race) someone ends up holding a folder of a few thousand photos. Everyone in those photos wants the handful they're in. The usual ways of handing th…
articles.body: After any big event (a wedding, a conference, a 10K race) someone ends up holding a folder of a few thousand photos. Everyone in those photos wants the handful they're in. The usual ways of handing them out are a shared Drive or Google Photos link, where everyone scrolls through everything and anyone with the link sees all of it, or a group-chat dump, where photos get buried and recompressed. Selfie search is the pattern a lot of event-photo tools have settled on: a guest takes one selfie, and the system returns only the photos that guest appears in. We build one of these tools, FotoNest. This post walks through how the flow works and, because it's what people actually ask about, what happens to the face data at each step.

articles.body: Originally published at neverpaytwice.pages.dev . Short answer: Claude Code writes each AI response to its log several times, and every copy carries the full token count. On the made-up sample log in our free scripts repo (30 responses, each logged 2 to 4 times, as Claude Code does), a plain sum says 5.3M tokens . The real figure is 1.8M . To get the right number, count each response once. Our free counter does that in your browser, or use the short script below. articles.title: Agentic AI Architectures: Building Deterministic Enterprise Systems Beyond Simple LLM Wrappers
articles.excerpt: The early wave of generative AI integrations across business software consisted almost entirely of "prompt-and-pray" wrappers: single-shot API calls to proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) instruc…
articles.body: The early wave of generative AI integrations across business software consisted almost entirely of "prompt-and-pray" wrappers: single-shot API calls to proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) instructed via long system prompts to produce JSON payloads. For interactive conversational chatbots or drafting blog intros, this approach was acceptable. For mission-critical enterprise workflows—such as reconciling bank statements, automating procurement orders, provisioning cloud access, or mutating ERP databases—it proved catastrophic. LLMs are probabilistic token prediction engines; enterprise systems demand deterministic guarantees.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.body: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15's booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its "Mechazilla" launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ' chopstick ' catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company's third-quarter earnings call that "success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight."
